absent: Construction of the per VCPU timer map, earliest expiry selection, wait for interrupt emulation detection, and helpers for enabled, pending, offsets, compare, control, save, emulate and interrupt update are not shown.

Host register programming details for offsets and compare and control resources, barrier semantics, tracing, and capability checks for host extensions, offsets, defective offsets, active state and nested contexts are not shown.

Virtual interrupt controller lookup, reference handling, initialization state, target selection, operations table, direct injection, generation detection and kernel controller presence checks are not shown.
Host interrupt numbers, flags, per CPU enable and disable, parent chip mask, unmask, end of interrupt and acknowledge behavior, and active state programming results beyond warning are not shown.

Default interrupt identifier table, controller specific translation, physical counter read, soft timer start and cancel, high resolution timer setup and expiry callbacks for emulation and background timers are not shown.
Protected virtual machine handling, counter offset flag, protection queries, and full reset values for all registers beyond control clearing are not shown.
Numeric values and layouts for control bits, trap bits, status bits, sysreg encodings and interrupt identifiers are not shown.

Remainder of host timer chip definition, interrupt domain allocation and free, domain operations, interrupt fixup and init, errata handling, hypervisor init, termination and validity checks are not shown because the final fragment is truncated.
Concurrency rules for timer contexts beyond virtual interrupt lock and preemption and interrupt guards, including interaction of load, put, blocking, expiry and nested transitions, are not shown.

findings.text: Lifecycle operations for per virtual CPU timer state are exposed for load, put, reset, init and synchronization. Load refreshes interrupt outputs, programs host active state, restores directly assigned timers, emulates others and configures traps. Put preserves directly assigned state, stops emulation and arms a background wakeup when the virtual CPU blocks. Reset clears controls and mapped interrupt state and stops emulation. Init establishes per timer contexts and background handling.

Guest register access for timers is provided through read and write helpers keyed by timer selector and register selector. Emulated timers are serviced from saved state with emulation refresh on writes. Directly assigned timers are serviced by preserving host register state around the access while preemption is held off. Supported selectors cover remaining count, control, compare, counter and virtual offset, with invalid selectors treated as fatal.

Virtual machine and CPU level initialization is exposed. Machine initialization assigns default per timer interrupt identifiers adjusted for interrupt controller generation. CPU initialization creates all timer contexts, synchronizes counter offsets unless already established or protected, and establishes background handling. CPU online and offline hooks enable and disable host timer interrupts.

Physical to virtual interrupt mapping queries and updates are exposed. Operations include testing whether a mapping is currently active, establishing a mapping from a host interrupt to a virtual identifier, clearing such a mapping, fetching the mapped hardware identifier, and resetting mapped active and pending state. Mapping establishment resolves the topmost parent hardware identifier and informs any direct injection hook.

Background wakeup is armed only when useful. If none of the mapped timer entries can raise a notification and no wait for interrupt trap emulation is active, the blocking path does nothing. Otherwise a single background timer is programmed to the earliest expiry across guest timers. The complementary unblocking path always cancels that background timer.

Restoration of directly assigned timer state is guarded and idempotent. It does nothing when the per CPU timer facility is disabled, serializes against host interrupts, and returns early when the context is already marked resident. Virtual family members program virtual offset and virtual compare and control resources, with a workaround for defective offset hardware that clears the offset register and folds the offset into the compare value. Physical family members program physical offset and physical compare and control resources. Completion is traced and the resident flag is set. An out of range timer selector is treated as fatal.

Loading timer state with a kernel interrupt controller first refreshes the virtual interrupt output from current pending state, then derives a host active indication as the logical OR of any existing hardware mapping active indication, the pending indication, and a generation indicator for the newest controller. The derived value is then programmed into the host interrupt controller active state for the context.

Without kernel interrupt controller active state support, load refreshes the virtual timer output from pending state and then directly controls the host virtual timer interrupt line. A pending output masks the host line to avoid repeated exits, while a clear output unmasks it so a future firing causes an exit.

On systems with kernel interrupt controller support, a nested transition exchanges emulated interrupt mappings for direct ones when the direct virtual mapping is absent. The path clears emulated virtual and physical mappings and then establishes direct virtual and physical mappings using each context host interrupt and virtual identifier, warning once on failure. It does nothing without a kernel interrupt controller.

Trap configuration for timer access applies only on host extension systems and otherwise returns. Default policy leaves all accesses untrapped, then selectively enables trapping for enhanced counter virtualization in hypervisor context with distinct bits for different execution modes, for nonzero physical offset without physical offset hardware, for nonzero virtual offset on defective offset hardware, and for nested guest hypervisor enable requests including redirected access bits. Requested trap and clear values are accumulated through a small predicate helper that sets one of two masks, then applied to the appropriate control register depending on nested virtualization capability.

Reset clears all timer controls to a disabled and unmasked value for every implemented timer, rebinds virtual offset pointers for nested execution to use the physical machine offset and the per virtual CPU offset register, clears virtual outputs, resets mapped interrupts for directly assigned timers when a kernel controller is present, and cancels emulation timers for emulated entries.

Per timer context initialization records the timer identity, selects a machine offset pointer based on timer family and protection state with no pointer for protected guests, establishes a monotonic absolute hard expiry handler, and assigns the host interrupt according to timer family. Virtual CPU initialization repeats this for all timers, initializes counter offsets from the physical counter for virtual and zero for physical unless protected or already established, and establishes the background timer handler.

Timer register read and write semantics are defined over five selectors. Remaining count is derived from stored compare, current physical count and offset and truncated to low half. Control read sets a status indication when no time remains regardless of enable. Compare and virtual offset reads return stored values, counter reads subtract offset from physical count. Writes update compare from physical count, offset and signed input for remaining count, update control with status bit masked out, update compare directly, or update virtual offset. Invalid selectors are fatal.

Host timer interrupt chip behavior forwards affinity changes to a per virtual CPU forwarding marker and always reports success. Active state changes pass through to the parent when not an active transition, when not forwarded, or on mixed controller generations, otherwise mask or unmask the parent based on the requested value. End of interrupt forwards to parent only when not forwarded to a virtual CPU. Acknowledge delegates to the parent acknowledge hook when present.

Access to mapping and active state in the virtual interrupt descriptor is serialized by the per interrupt lock held with host interrupts saved. This covers testing active mapping, establishing and clearing hardware mappings, fetching the hardware identifier, and resetting active, latch and level indications. References acquired for lookup are released after unlock.

Direct timer register preservation across reads and writes is performed with preemption disabled, and restoration of host timer registers is performed with host interrupts saved. Emulated timer accesses do not take the preservation path.

Observed per CPU timer state carries an enabled flag and a background timer object. Observed per timer context carries an identity, a resident flag, a host interrupt number, an emulation timer object, and offset pointers for virtual CPU and machine scope. Offsets and control, compare and counter values are accessed through helpers.

Observed virtual interrupt state carries a hardware mapping flag, a host interrupt number, a hardware identifier, active, latch and level indications, a lock, a target virtual CPU reference, and an optional operations table with a direct injection hook. Mapping sets the flag, host number and hardware identifier. Unmapping clears the flag and identifier and disables direct injection.

Observed host timer interrupt chip state provides a name and callbacks for acknowledge, end of interrupt, active state programming and affinity. The acknowledge callback is wired to parent delegation and the chip is registered as the timer interrupt handler.

Virtual CPU timer residency follows load, resident, put and blocked phases. Load cancels any background wakeup and marks direct contexts resident while starting emulation for emulated entries. Put preserves direct state, stops emulation and, when blocking, arms a single background wakeup to the earliest expiry. Unblocking or a subsequent load cancels the wakeup. Reset leaves emulation stopped.

Each virtual CPU timer access selects between direct host register use and software emulation based on a per virtual CPU map distinguishing direct and emulated virtual and physical entries, with direct physical possibly absent. Direct entries use save and restore around host registers. Emulated entries use cancellation plus emulation refresh. Nested transitions can exchange which entries are direct.

Hardware mapping lifecycle moves between unmapped, mapped idle, mapped active and reset states. Establishing a mapping sets hardware indication and identifier and enables direct injection when supported. Clearing disables direct injection and clears indication and identifier. Reset clears active, latch and level while leaving the mapping flag intact, and is a no-op when no hardware mapping exists.

Virtual CPU transition entry points drive timer behavior on scheduling, blocking, reset and synchronization. Scheduling in restores and emulates, scheduling out preserves and optionally arms wakeup, reset reinitializes, user synchronization unmasks when needed, and nested synchronization refreshes emulation when trap support is unavailable.

CPU and interrupt subsystem entry points include online and offline hooks that enable or disable host timer lines, and interrupt chip callbacks invoked on affinity change, active state change, end of interrupt and acknowledge.

A timer may expire after the virtual output has been refreshed but before host registers are restored. The design accepts this race because the pending interrupt will still be taken, so no lost wakeup handling is required in the load paths.

With a userspace interrupt controller and host support lacking active state, a continuously asserted virtual level would cause repeated exits without progress. The implementation masks the host line while pending and unmasks on deassertion, and provides a user synchronization path that clears output and unmasks when no longer pending.

Several invalid conditions are treated as fatal or error returns. An out of range timer index in restore or register access traps. A missing descriptor for a host interrupt during mapping logs and returns an invalid argument indication. Mapping operations assert descriptor presence. Unmapping without initialization returns a retry indication, and active testing without initialization reports inactive.

Control register status semantics are defined so expiry is indicated by a status bit that reads as set when no time remains even with enable clear, and writes mask this bit out so guest writes cannot set it directly.
Emulation and background timers use a monotonic clock with absolute hard expiry mode.
Host active state programming uses the interrupt chip active state identifier. A nonzero result from programming is treated as a warning condition.

User interrupt controller synchronization only acts when timers are enabled and no kernel controller is present. It checks the virtual timer pending state and, when clear, clears the virtual output and either deactivates host active state where supported or re-enables the host virtual line.

Nested synchronization without enhanced counter trap support cancels emulation timers for emulated entries and re-runs emulation on every guest exit to account for guest hypervisor updates hidden by memory redirection. With trap support the path does nothing.

Mapping queries report inactive when the controller is uninitialized, otherwise return the conjunction of hardware indication and active indication under lock, or return the hardware identifier when mapped and a negative sentinel otherwise.
